nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-02.title: Multiplication principle
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-02.body:
Each of the four digits can be chosen in $2$ ways, so there are $2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2 = 16$ plates.

**Answer: 16**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-03.title: Clear the denominator
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-03.body:
$x^2 - 1 = 3(x - 1)$ gives $x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0$, $(x-1)(x-2) = 0$. The root $x = 1$ makes the denominator $0$, so only $x = 2$ works.

**Answer: $x = 2$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-04.title: Exponents
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-04.body:
Each square root halves the exponent: $\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt2}}} = 2^{1/16}$. So $\log_2 2^{1/16} = \frac1{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{16}$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-04.title: Peel off one root at a time

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-05.title: One set of coins
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-05.body:
One penny, nickel, dime and quarter together are worth $1 + 5 + 10 + 25 = 41$ cents. With $x$ of each coin, $41x = 164$, so $x = 4$.

**Answer: 4 pennies**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-05.title: Look at the pennies
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-05.body:
The amount ends in $4$ cents, and the other coins are worth multiples of $5$ cents, so the number of pennies is $4$ or $9$ or more. Nine of each coin would include nine quarters, $\$2.25$, too much. So she has $4$ pennies (and $4\cdot41 = 164$ cents checks).

**Answer: 4 pennies**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-06.title: Divide the terms
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-06.body:
With first term $a$ and ratio $r$: $ar = 6$ and $ar^4 = 162$. Dividing, $r^3 = 27$, so $r = 3$ (the only real cube root), and $a = 2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-06.title: Step through the terms
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-06.body:
From the second term to the fifth term we multiply by $r$ three times: $6r^3 = 162$, $r = 3$. The terms are $2, 6, 18, 54, 162$, so the first term is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-07.title: Pair the divisors
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-07.body:
If $d$ divides $1200$, so does $\frac{1200}{d}$, and since $1200$ is not a perfect square the $30$ divisors split into $15$ pairs with product $1200$ each. The product of all divisors is $1200^{15} = (12\cdot10^2)^{15} = 12^{15}\cdot10^{30}$. Because $12^a10^b = 2^{2a+b}3^a5^b$, the exponents are unique: $(a,b) = (15,30)$.

**Answer: $(15,30)$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-07.title: Prime exponents
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-07.body:
$1200 = 2^4\cdot3\cdot5^2$. In the product of all $30$ divisors, each prime appears with exponent (sum of its exponents over the divisors): for $3$, half the divisors contain $3^1$, giving $15$; for $5$, the exponents $0,1,2$ each occur in $10$ divisors, giving $30$; for $2$, the exponents $0,\dots,4$ each occur in $6$ divisors, giving $60$. So the product is $2^{60}3^{15}5^{30}$. Matching $2^{2a+b}3^a5^b$: $a = 15$, $b = 30$ (and $2a + b = 60$ checks).

**Answer: $(15,30)$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-08.title: Overlap of two segments
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-08.body:
$AX = 6$ and $BY = 8$ lie along $AB = 10$ from opposite ends. Their lengths add to $14$, which exceeds $10$ by the overlap $XY$. So $XY = 6 + 8 - 10 = 4$.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-08.title: Coordinates on the line
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-08.body:
Put $A$ at $0$ and $B$ at $10$ on a number line. Then $X = 6$ and $Y = 10 - 8 = 2$, so $XY = 4$.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-09.title: Sum of the roots
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-09.body:
The sum of the roots of $x^2 - px + q = 0$ is $p$. So $p = \sin^2 17^\circ + \cos^2 17^\circ = 1$.

**Answer: 1**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-10.title: Inclusion-exclusion
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-10.body:
Among $1, \dots, 200$: multiples of $2$: $100$; of $3$: $66$; of $5$: $40$; of $6$: $33$; of $10$: $20$; of $15$: $13$; of $30$: $6$. The numbers divisible by at least one of $2, 3, 5$ number $100 + 66 + 40 - 33 - 20 - 13 + 6 = 146$. So $200 - 146 = 54$ are divisible by none.

**Answer: 54**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-10.title: Blocks of 30
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-10.body:
In each block of $30$ consecutive numbers, exactly $\varphi(30) = 8$ are coprime to $30$ (namely those $\equiv 1, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29 \pmod{30}$). $1$ to $180$ has $6$ blocks: $48$ numbers. From $181$ to $200$ the residues $1, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19$ add $6$ more. Total $54$.

**Answer: 54**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-11.title: Circumradius to side
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-11.body:
$\pi R^2 = 12\pi$ gives $R = 2\sqrt3$. In an equilateral triangle the circumradius is $\frac{s}{\sqrt3}$, so $s = R\sqrt3 = 6$. The area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot 36 = 9\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $9\sqrt3$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-11.title: Three central triangles
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-11.body:
The center splits the triangle into three congruent triangles with two sides $R$ and included angle $120^\circ$. The area is $3\cdot\frac12R^2\sin120^\circ = \frac32\cdot12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = 9\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $9\sqrt3$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-12.title: Remainder theorem
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-12.body:
The remainder on division by $x - 3$ is the value at $x = 3$: $27 - 9 + 5k - 2 = 16 + 5k$. Setting $16 + 5k = k$ gives $k = -4$.

**Answer: $-4$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-13.title: Net winnings
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-13.body:
Every game has a winner. Boris won $4$ games, so Bobby lost $4$ games and paid $4$ dollars. If Bobby won $w$ games, his net gain is $w - 4 = 4$, so $w = 8$. In all they played $4 + 8 = 12$ games.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-13.title: Reading 'won 4 dollars' as dollars collected
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-13.body:
Bobby collects one dollar for each game he wins. If the $4$ dollars he has won means the money he collected, then Bobby won $4$ games. Together with Boris's $4$ wins, they played $4 + 4 = 8$ games.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-16.title: Quadratic formula
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-16.body:
The roots are $\frac{-9 \pm \sqrt{81 - 48}}{2}$, and their difference is $\sqrt{33}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{33}$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-17.title: Track both hands
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-17.body:
At 5:15 the minute hand points at the 3, i.e. $90^\circ$ from 12. The hour hand moves $30^\circ$ per hour, so it is at $5\cdot30^\circ + \frac14\cdot30^\circ = 157.5^\circ$. The angle between them is $157.5^\circ - 90^\circ = 67.5^\circ$.

**Answer: $67.5^\circ$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-17.title: Start from 5:00
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-17.body:
At 5:00 the hands are $150^\circ$ apart. In $15$ minutes the minute hand gains $15\cdot(6^\circ - 0.5^\circ) = 82.5^\circ$ on the hour hand, leaving $150^\circ - 82.5^\circ = 67.5^\circ$.

**Answer: $67.5^\circ$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-19.title: Use the rule twice
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-19.body:
Box $1$ holds slip $3$. By the rule with $n = 1$, the slip in box $1$ (which is $3$) is the number of the box containing slip $1$, so box $3$ holds slip $1$. The only slip left is $2$, which goes in box $2$. Check: box $2$ holds slip $2$, and slip $2$ is in box $2$, consistent with the rule.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-20.title: Double-angle formula
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-20.body:
$\cos^2 A = 1 - \frac{9}{25} = \frac{16}{25}$ and $\cos A > 0$, so $\cos A = \frac45$. Then $\sin2A = 2\sin A\cos A = 2\cdot\frac35\cdot\frac45 = \frac{24}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac{24}{25}$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-20.title: 3-4-5 triangle
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-20.body:
Take $A$ as an acute angle of a right triangle with legs $3$ (opposite) and $4$ (adjacent) and hypotenuse $5$. Then $\cos A = \frac45$ and $\sin 2A = 2\cdot\frac35\cdot\frac45 = \frac{24}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac{24}{25}$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-21.title: Use divisibility by 5 and 9
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-21.body:
A multiple of $45$ is a multiple of $5$, so its last digit is $0$ or $5$. The digits increase, so the last digit is the largest and cannot be $0$: it is $5$. The candidates are $135$ (difference $2$) and $345$ (difference $1$). A multiple of $9$ has digit sum divisible by $9$: $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$ works, $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ does not. So the number is $135 = 45\cdot3$.

**Answer: 135**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-23.title: Equal tangent lengths
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-23.body:
Let the tangent lengths from $A$, $B$, $C$ be $z$, $x$, $y$ (the two tangents from a point to a circle are equal, so $BP$ is the tangent length $x$ from $B$). Then $x + y = BC = 7$, $y + z = AC = 6$, $x + z = AB = 11$. Adding, $x + y + z = 12$, so $x = 12 - 6 = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-23.title: Semiperimeter formula
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-23.body:
The tangent length from $B$ equals $s - AC$, where $s = \frac{11 + 6 + 7}{2} = 12$. So $BP = 12 - 6 = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-24.title: Vieta
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-24.body:
Let the roots be $r$ and $3r$ with $r > 0$. Their product is $3r^2 = 24$, so $r = 2\sqrt2$, and the roots are $2\sqrt2$ and $6\sqrt2$. Then $p$ is their sum, $8\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $8\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-24.title: Substitute
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-24.body:
From $r + 3r = p$, $r = \frac p4$, and the product gives $3\cdot\frac{p^2}{16} = 24$, so $p^2 = 128$. Positive roots require $p > 0$, so $p = 8\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $8\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-25.title: Greedy construction
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-25.body:
An odd multiple of $5$ ends in $5$. With distinct digits the number has at most $10$ digits, and using all ten digits gives the largest numbers. With $5$ fixed in the units place, put the remaining digits in decreasing order: $9876432105$.

**Answer: 9876432105**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-27.title: Write in base 9
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-27.body:
$3^{12} = 9^6$, which is $1\,000\,000_9$. Subtracting $3$ (borrowing nines) gives $888\,886_9$. The last two digits are $86$.

**Answer: 86**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-27.title: Remainder mod 81
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-27.body:
The last two base-9 digits are determined by the remainder mod $81$. $3^{12} - 3 \equiv -3 \equiv 78 \pmod{81}$, and $78 = 8\cdot9 + 6$, so the digits are $8, 6$.

**Answer: 86**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-28.title: Set up an equation
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-28.body:
With $n$ pages per volume, the first pages are $1$, $n + 1$, $2n + 1$. So $3n + 3 = 1353$ and $n = 450$.

**Answer: 450 pages**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-28.title: Average first page
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-28.body:
The three first pages form an arithmetic progression with middle term $\frac{1353}{3} = 451$. The middle volume starts at page $n + 1 = 451$, so $n = 450$.

**Answer: 450 pages**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-29.title: Pigeonhole on last digits
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-29.body:
Two numbers differ by a multiple of $10$ exactly when they have the same remainder mod $10$ (same last digit). There are $10$ remainders, so at most $10$ numbers; $1, 2, \dots, 10$ shows $10$ is possible.

**Answer: 10**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-30.title: Difference of squares
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-30.body:
Let $n + 201 = a^2$ and $n + 125 = b^2$ with $a > b \ge 0$. Then $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b) = 76$. The factors have the same parity, so both are even: $a - b = 2$, $a + b = 38$, giving $a = 20$, $b = 18$ (the pairs $1\cdot76$ and $4\cdot19$ have mixed parity). Then $n = 18^2 - 125 = 199$, the only positive solution.

**Answer: 199**

nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-30.title: Gaps between squares
nyciml-1984-85-spring-seniorb-30.body:
Write the larger square as $(b+k)^2$ with $k \ge 1$, so $(b+k)^2 - b^2 = 2kb + k^2 = 76$. Since $76$ is even, $k$ is even, and $k^2 < 76$ gives $k \le 8$. Then $k = 2$: $4b + 4 = 76$, $b = 18$; $k = 4$: $8b = 60$; $k = 6$: $12b = 40$; $k = 8$: $16b = 12$; only $k = 2$ gives an integer. So $b^2 = 324$ and $n = 324 - 125 = 199$.

**Answer: 199**
